nameStory: The Greater Moon Jelly gets its name from its translucent, moon-like bell that glows ethereally as it pulses through the water. Like other moon jellies, its rounded, ghostly appearance reminded early observers of the full moon floating beneath the waves. The 'greater' part of its name refers to its impressive size compared to its more common cousin.
description: The Greater Moon Jelly is a large, translucent jellyfish with a saucer-shaped bell that can reach up to 18 inches across. Its jelly-like body is nearly transparent with a subtle bluish or whitish tint, making it appear almost ghostly in the water. Four distinctive horseshoe-shaped reproductive organs are visible through the bell, creating a cloverleaf pattern at the center. This impressive cnidarian (a group that includes jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones) propels itself through gentle, rhythmic contractions of its bell.

idTips.label: Scalloped Bell Edge
idTips.description: The bell margin has 16 distinct inward curves or scallops, creating a gently wavy edge rather than a smooth circle when viewed from above

idTips.label: Large Size
idTips.description: Notably large for a moon jelly, often exceeding 12 inches across with specimens reaching up to 18 inches in diameter

idTips.label: Transparent Bell
idTips.description: Body feels like firm jello and appears nearly see-through with a subtle milky or bluish tinge, allowing you to see through to the other side

idTips.label: Four-Leaf Clover Pattern
idTips.description: Four horseshoe or kidney-shaped structures visible through the bell form a distinctive cloverleaf pattern at the center

idTips.label: Gentle Pulsing Movement
idTips.description: Moves with slow, rhythmic contractions of the bell, creating a hypnotic pumping motion as it drifts through the water

habitat: Greater Moon Jellies are extremely rare visitors to New England waters, as they primarily live in the northeastern Pacific Ocean from California to Alaska. The single observation in New England likely represents an unusual stray or misidentification. They typically inhabit coastal waters, harbors, and bays where they drift with currents and tides.

seasonality.spring: Not typically present in New England waters during spring, as this is a Pacific species.
seasonality.summer: Any potential sightings would most likely occur during warmer summer months when water temperatures are highest.
seasonality.fall: Not expected in New England waters during fall months.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters in winter due to cold temperatures and their Pacific Ocean range.

funFact: Greater Moon Jellies are living time machines - they have no brain, heart, or blood, yet they've survived for over 500 million years using the same basic body plan, making them older than dinosaurs, trees, and even fish!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with the much more common Moon Jelly (Aurelia aurita), but Greater Moon Jellies are typically larger and may have slightly different proportions. However, given their rarity in New England, any moon jelly sighting is far more likely to be the common species.
contextualKnowledge: The single observation of Greater Moon Jelly in New England is highly unusual since this species is native to Pacific waters. This could represent a rare stray that somehow crossed continents, a specimen transported by human activity, or potentially a misidentification of the similar Common Moon Jelly.
compareHints: Greater Moon Jellies are typically larger than Common Moon Jellies, though their size ranges overlap significantly. Both species can have 16-scalloped bell edges, making them very difficult to distinguish without genetic analysis. The most reliable difference is geographic location - Greater Moon Jellies belong on the Pacific coast, while Common Moon Jellies are the species you'd expect to encounter in New England waters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Common Moon Jelly differs from its close relatives by its specific four-horseshoe pattern and North Atlantic location.
Southern Moon Jellies are virtually indistinguishable from Common Moon Jellies by appearance alone - both share the telltale four horseshoe-shaped reproductive organs and crystal-clear bell.
